extract.title: Sustaining Human Knowledge: A Manifesto from the MIT Epistemic Futures Summit

principles.statement: Stop counting papers: funders, governments and universities must drop paper- and citation-based metrics and rankings, assess demonstrated judgment, and impose enforceable correction and retraction duties on publishers.
Treat credibility as maintained infrastructure by funding checkers as a commons through a pooled endowment, paid as a body, with checkers ratifying key schemas and payers barred from governing.
Nobody should grade their own homework: audits must be independent of those who profit from them, AI releases must publish error rates, and accountable organizations must carry liability insurance.
Signals should send people to check rather than stand in for checking, with blind first readings, claim-level trails, and cues tested on trusted community intermediaries, not just lab readers.
Design against smoothness: AI-mediated answers should show disagreement, null results and dead ends, route to conflicting sources, and be tested against the verdict alone.
A human in the loop is not a safeguard by itself; first decide openly whether AI belongs at all, keep final checks with people, and require designs to beat human and AI alone.

Build competence before reliance, judge tools by what competence remains when removed, fund longitudinal studies, and place responsibility on institutions through defaults and conditions rather than warnings.

Pay for the human knowledge models depend on, give producers an antitrust safe harbour to bargain collectively, and require disclosed provenance, short-term licences and independently audited usage reporting.

Keep the record open and forkable, respect community consent (CARE), require attribution and identified crawlers, disclose automation and concealed sponsorship, never identify readers, and constrain registries.
Infrastructure is governance, so excluded communities, including the Global South and ordinary users, must be seated with paid, binding say before categories are fixed, and refusal must be fundable.

commitments: Funders will remove paper counts and citation metrics from grants, hiring and promotion, attach audits, failure records, tool-removal tests and provenance-and-consent statements to grants, and audit compliance.
Together the signatories will charter the checking commons, starting by measuring volunteer checking labour with volunteer communities co-designing and ratifying the measure.
Before setting any payment formula, they will test with volunteer communities whether pay strengthens or crowds out obligation and publish the results either way.
The organizers will co-convene the next summit with excluded groups, pay their costs, give each binding say over categories, and report whether authority shifted.
Companies among the signatories will pay in and not govern.
Katherine Maher reaffirmed NPR's commitment that nothing put before its audience is AI-produced and committed that any NPR licensing will charge for access, never for the integrity signal.
Adam Bly will take CC0 on data plus patent non-assertion to System's board and report within six months, hold System's finding schema outside System, and allow independent audits.
Esther Dyson pledged her own money.
Jason Priem committed OpenAlex to removing community curation from paid tiers on an announced date, publishing curation rules and correction logs, mirroring outside the US, and keeping data CC0.
James Evans committed Knowledge Lab to an open retrospective benchmark of evaluators and to helping seed the negative-results commons.
Builders will publish per-release error rates, submit to independent audit, and test mitigations against the human alone and machine alone.
Institutions will fund paid first jobs, apprenticeships, tool-withdrawal studies and protected mentoring time, and report how many early-career people they trained and kept.
The organizers will approach non-US public funders and foundations to seed an endowment and within six months publish whom they approached, sums offered and sources, and the remaining gap.

extract.title: Keep Disagreement Visible: A Manifesto for Sustaining Human Knowledge

principles.statement: Keep disagreement visible by showing named, sourced positions where experts disagree, maintaining many models including open-weight ones, and budgeting payouts for least-retrieved sources rather than collapsing into one confident answer.

Count independent routes to evidence rather than repetitions, carry claim-level provenance showing lineage independence without scoring it, federate graphs, and never make being counted the condition for being trusted.

Cite by default with openable links, reward link-backs, test citations for support and fair representation, disclose who built systems, and make high-stakes systems fully open to independent auditors and authorities.

Record failures and negative knowledge as first-class data, report failure events by model version, bound reliance where error sources are untraceable, and pay for nulls, replications, corrections and checking.

Audit model behavior independently of vendors with versioned behavioral tests and archived baselines, forbid AI grading AI, require liable insured owners for services, and provide ways to contest AI-based overrides.

Build human competence before reliance by redesigning situations and inviting people into checking work, with policies on learning sequence and tests comparing competence-first and tool-first cohorts.

Fix pre-AI incentives upstream by certifying practiced checking, enforcing DORA in grant review, holding publishers to retraction standards, publishing misconduct reports, and funding sleuths by retainer with legal defense.

Collect fine-grained open telemetry on agent operators where money changes hands, allocate money coarsely through coalitions to those sustaining the record, and fund it by a levy on firms that took work without permission.

Treat open-to-read as distinct from open-to-train, require author opt-in for training on in-copyright scholarship, keep deals short, respect existing licences like Wikipedia's, and fund refusal as legitimate.

Every body that counts, collects, funds or validates must bind itself in advance through a Ulysses pact with open governance, forkability, sunset clauses, annual outside-reviewed self-assessments and sustainable funding.
Every recommendation must name who acts or be recorded as unowned, with a public report by September 2027 checking commitments and returning slipped items to the unowned column.

extract.title: People, Not Data: A Manifesto for Sustaining Human Knowledge

principles.statement: Fund the people who check knowledge (curators, sleuths, evaluators, mentors, readers) as infrastructure, name owners for training newcomers, and make apprenticeship a line item in grants and AI contracts.
Build skill before reliance on tools, test the competence-collapse model experimentally, test human seats without the tool, and assess understanding rather than credentials.

Answers should cite sources by default, show cited passages and correction status, reveal thin evidence, invite click-through, and institutions should mandate this in contracts with independent traffic counts.

Judge authority by correction speed; every public agent needs an accountable, insured party, with insurers priced on independent records, audited by regulators, and small players exempted or subsidized.
Favor plurality by showing competing named positions, counting only independent sources, testing signals on real readers, and requiring gatekeeping reviewers to pass a society-held novelty test.

Build accountable institutions with adversarial review, give final checks to diverse accountable panels, use lookup-based AI for verification, audit all seats against measured floors, and fund open verification.

Audit system behavior, not statements, using shared bias batteries, training checkpoints, data disclosure and public bias registers, preserve retired models, and document error classes in an open taxonomy.

Extractors should pay communities based on audited provenance, not per-sentence meters or citation counts, while funders drop paper counts and fund review, bounties, negative results and fast corrections.
Honour community-chosen licences, never opt in communities that haven't chosen, require reciprocity via pooled funds and a commons-rent backstop tax, allow collective bargaining, and build public AI.

Counting infrastructure should be open, forkable, independently overseen including those described, endowment-funded, with full funding disclosure, Southern governance from day one, and published costs to small journals.

extract.title: Pay for the People Who Check: A Manifesto for Sustaining Human Knowledge

principles.statement: Fund early-career and volunteer human checkers rather than machines, require checking roles to prove impact, bar models from gating decisions until tested on novel claims, and publish fixes openly.

Funders and institutions should stop using counts of papers, citations and retrievals in hiring, promotion and funding by a named year, and credit curation, correction, mentoring and negative results instead.

Scholarly AI answers must show fair, audited, checkable sources, flag thin or conflicting evidence, check retraction status automatically, display disagreements, and disclose link-hallucination rates.

AI checking tools must be independently auditable, with no self-grading or count-based auditor pay, published failure catalogues, bias testing across checkpoints, and a public registry with consequences.

Redesign situations rather than relying on warnings: hide polish cues, make provenance easy to inspect, reduce checker bias, and field-test interventions like explain-first designs before mandating them.
Institutions must ensure competence is built before reliance on AI, fund tests of the dependence model, practise oversight with and without tools, and require employers to fund entry-level mentoring.

Ensure plural, independent origins of knowledge by exposing coordinated seeding operations while protecting anonymity, checking diversity of corpora and checkers, and funding negative knowledge and places for collective checking.

AI firms using the commons must pay to sustain it through coarse, non-per-use payments, separate training and grounding controls, collective bargaining for checkers, and a publicly held commons-rent levy fund.

Every rule must name its policer, payer, accountable outside overruler and review date, assume capture, guarantee exit through openness, keep makers liable, and give Southern infrastructures voting co-design seats.

commitments: We will ask whether a tool belongs, never mandate AI, allow declining without reason, and run open community-governed tools on university servers as the default where no vendor passes our tests.

We will reconvene in a year with a named payer, co-stewarding regional and early-career voters, funded sleuths, and a dated non-ranking dashboard tracking money, checking, overrulers and second-order effects.
OpenAttribution (Alex Springer) pledges free repository membership, CDN-free log witnessing, a verification design before pricing, an outside-funded audit and crawler-only registration.
OpenAlex (Jason Priem) pledges a self-audit, a running non-US mirror, open retraction flags and corrections, and no rankings built on its data.
System (Adam Bly) pledges written patent non-assertion, an outside extraction audit, a published clinical overreliance study and a board answer on its licence.
Wikimedia pledges crawler edge logs and a measure of whether AI-referred readers edit.
Microsoft (Brent Hecht) pledges an outside audit of Copilot's citation fidelity with binding cost-sharing.
NPR (Katherine Maher) pledges no AI-made content and published licences buying audit rights, paid correctors and usage-independent local-news money.
O'Reilly pledges auditable royalty logic.
Nick Vincent pledges a safe-harbour memo and an audit-layer specification.
David Krakauer pledges designs for both Principle 6 tests, stating what would refute hysteresis.
Esther Dyson pledges rules for liability insurance priced from the audit layer.
James Evans pledges a novelty test, a null-results pilot and a non-ranking concentration index.

We will fund tests before mandates, including tool removal in both orders, explain-first designs, dropping the first-person "I", machine novelty recognition and lateral reading, and give this manifesto its own review date.

principles.statement: Stop using publication counts and rankings as proxies for productivity in funding and policy, and make corrections earn rather than cost journal reputation.

AI systems that depend on the commons should fund it and disclose sources; training on in-copyright books needs opt-in consent, and AI answers should log retrieved and cited sources via an open audited standard.
Build an open, complete record where corrections are first-class data, require timely correction deposits, check citations against it by default, and fund sleuths and open null-result commons.

AI tools should give sourced maps of expert agreement and disagreement rather than single answers, verify citations externally, count independent sources, show claim origins, and register agents to accountable owners.
Fund checking through a POSI-compliant, co-governed pool paying for practice rather than per item, with owed multi-year dues, wind-down reserves, independent oversight, and no single-country control.
A missing signal must never count against those who cannot afford to send it; keep participation free for small and Southern presses and open community knowledge only on negotiated, reversible terms.

Nobody should grade their own work: no model audits itself, measure model independence, gate automated reviewers behind published tests, maintain an outside bias registry, and publish failure classes.

Redesign situations with named owners rather than relying on warnings; bar first-person address, simulated emotion and AI companions for children; and make assessment require demonstrated understanding, tested over time.
Build human competence before reliance on AI, treat unrebuilt output as unverified, fund training of new error-checkers and withdrawal tests, and keep mentored entry-level roles.

commitments: Stop counting papers and stop using rankings in funding.
Write these rules and guaranteed exit into every AI contract, with co-governed regional addenda, no forced Northern identifiers or metrics, and several funded community-governed tools.
Pay owed dues into the pool.

Bargain as one coalition including data workers and annotators, seek safe harbors without depending on any one, give non-members charter seats, keep research use free, and publish an outside cartel-risk review before pricing.
Name one owner for each rule.
Fund the head-to-head and withdrawal tests, measuring lost skill and absorbed bias behaviorally.
Red-team against small presses, diamond journals and Indigenous archives before adoption, and scale no payment scheme until those tests and market modeling are published.
Jason Priem commits OpenAlex corrections data, an independent auditor and mirrors outside the US.
Adam Bly commits to the auditor test and to taking System's licence to his board.
Brent Hecht's group commits to a retrieved-versus-cited audit.

principles.statement: Distinguish what was already broken, what AI is breaking, and what is moral panic, and give each category its own remedy rather than blaming everything or nothing on AI.

telemetry.label: partial
telemetry.evidence: The telemetry itself should be audited by rotating auditors not paid by the labs.

antitrust_safe_harbour.label: partial
antitrust_safe_harbour.evidence: it would need producers bargaining jointly under an antitrust safe harbour (Farrell, Hecht, Vincent, Brand, Maher)

levy.label: partial
levy.evidence: A firm-level, revenue-based levy drew broad support, but not settled support.

training_vs_grounding.label: dissent_only
training_vs_grounding.evidence: Grounding and training should have separate consent controls.

consent_to_train.label: dissent_only
consent_to_train.evidence: Consent remained split: Becker, Brand and Dash put consent first.

honour_licences.label: dissent_only
honour_licences.evidence: Labs training on Wikipedia while Wikimedia pays the infrastructure bill is "Napster, not a commons." They should pay for the load.

refusal_fundable.label: endorsed
refusal_fundable.evidence: Chan added that refusal should be a fundable choice for communities.

forkable_infrastructure.label: partial
forkable_infrastructure.evidence: A fork protects only if someone can afford to run it (Weinberger, Deckelmann, Dyson), which led to Bilder's funder-backed exit insurance pool.

profiting_counter.label: dissent_only
profiting_counter.evidence: The measurement should never be set by the party that takes a margin on the count.

southern_governance.label: dissent_only
southern_governance.evidence: Levy funds should be governed by the people who get summarized.

identify_agents_not_readers.label: dissent_only
identify_agents_not_readers.evidence: She asked that human traffic come first and that crawlers identify themselves.

failure_data.label: partial
failure_data.evidence: They included null-result collection (Evans)

charter_for_every_body.label: endorsed
charter_for_every_body.evidence: every mechanism must say who polices it, who pays, and who guards the guards.

environmental_costs.label: dissent_only
environmental_costs.evidence: Automation does not remove human labour. It moves it into curating data, and that labour is currently invisible.

apprenticeship.label: endorsed
apprenticeship.evidence: apprenticeships for the next generation of checkers (Krakauer)

absent_voices.label: partial
absent_voices.evidence: the funders who would have to act were not present.
